title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about generative AI: what it is, what it can and cannot do, and how to use it honestly in your studies. By the end you will be able to explain in plain terms what a tool like a chatbot really is, describe where it is reliable and where it is not, and recognise how to use it with academic integrity.

Tools like ChatGPT are now part of student life, and knowing what they actually do matters. Understanding how they work, where they go wrong, and how to use them honestly protects your learning and your marks, whatever you are studying.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain in plain terms what generative AI is and how it produces its output
describe what generative AI can and cannot reliably do, and why its output can be wrong
recognise how to use AI tools honestly and with academic integrity in your studies.

title: In real academic practice
body: Across the School of Sport, AI tools now sit alongside your reading, your reports and your revision, whether you study sport science, coaching, management or therapy. Knowing what they are and how they fail lets you use them as a help rather than a hazard, and using them honestly keeps your analysis your own. Treat what follows as being about your own sport work: the studies you read, the reports you write, and the declarations your course asks for, not about study in the abstract.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what generative AI is: what the tool actually does when you type a prompt. Second, what AI can and cannot do: where it is useful and why a confident answer can still be wrong. Third, using AI with integrity: how to work with these tools honestly. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, tools and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You have probably typed a question into a chatbot and used the answer it gave back. Before you let a tool like that near your assessments at Cardiff Met, two things matter: understanding what it actually is, and knowing the one rule that decides whether you may use it at all. This lesson covers both.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies and are not expected to know how these tools are built. The aim is simpler: understand in plain terms what generative AI is, meet the single principle that keeps your use of it honest, and see that your Cardiff Met assignment brief decides what is allowed.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe, in plain terms, what generative AI is and why it can be confidently wrong
state the one rule - that whatever you submit must show your own understanding and judgement
recognise that your Cardiff Met assignment brief decides which of three categories of AI use applies in sport.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Generative AI is a kind of computer tool that produces new content, usually text but also images, audio or code, in response to a prompt you type. A chatbot like ChatGPT is the most familiar example: you ask it something, and it writes back an answer in ordinary language.

The key thing to understand is how it produces that answer. It is not searching a library for a stored fact, and it is not thinking the way a person does. It has been trained on huge amounts of text, and it works by predicting, one piece at a time, the words most likely to come next. The result reads as if a knowledgeable person wrote it, but underneath it is pattern prediction, not understanding.

title: Concept: in practice
body: At Cardiff Met, as at any university, one rule governs everything. Whatever you submit for assessment must show your own understanding and judgement. Because a chatbot predicts likely wording rather than understanding your topic, its answer is not your understanding, so handing it in as your own breaks that rule. Cardiff Met's Academic Handbook is clear that your assignment brief decides whether, and how, you may use AI. If the brief does not say AI is allowed, treat it as not allowed, and ask your tutor if you are unsure. Cardiff Met sets out three categories of AI use - no AI expected, AI acknowledged, and AI embedded - and your brief tells you which applies. The next lesson works through them.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The key term
body: Select the card to reveal the term, then step through its meaning.
instruction: Select the card to reveal each part.
definition: A computer tool that creates new text, images or other content by predicting likely patterns, rather than storing or looking up facts.
extendedDefinition: A generative AI tool such as a chatbot is trained on large amounts of text and produces an answer by predicting, piece by piece, what is most likely to come next. It generates fluent language, but it does not understand what it writes or check it against the truth.
example: Ask a chatbot to explain a topic and it writes a fresh answer by predicting likely wording, not by copying one stored source.

title: Explore AI literacy
displayTitle: The four levels of AI literacy
body:
AI literacy means knowing what AI can do, where it falls short, and how to use it fairly. It also means seeing the risks, such as bias, weak privacy, copyright questions and the environmental cost.

One test runs through all of it. Who is doing the thinking here, you or the tool? Lean on AI too hard and you miss the chance to build the skills employers look for.
instruction: Open any level to read it. You can keep more than one open at once.

_items.title: Basic: knowing what AI is
_items.body:
You understand what generative AI is and roughly how it works. A chatbot predicts likely words from patterns in the text it was trained on. It does not look things up or know what is true, so it can sound confident and still be wrong.

At this level you can use the basic terms, such as prompt, model and training data, and you treat AI as a tool, not an expert.
_items.advice: This means you can explain, in plain words, what a chatbot is doing when it answers, and why a fluent reply is not proof that the facts are right.

_items.title: Intermediate: using AI to learn
_items.body:
You use AI tools effectively to support your study and to solve problems. You might ask it to explain a tricky concept, plan your time, quiz you for practice, or comment on a draft where your brief allows it.

At this level you write clearer prompts, give the tool context, and follow up to go deeper, so the work still builds your own understanding.
_items.advice: This means you reach for AI to help you think, not to think for you, and you can always say what you learned from the exchange.

_items.title: Advanced: evaluating the output
_items.body:
You judge what a tool gives you rather than trusting it. You check its claims for accuracy, watch for bias and missing viewpoints, and test facts against reliable sources.

You also weigh the wider issues, such as privacy, data protection, copyright and the environmental cost, and you recognise when using AI would cross a line.
_items.advice: This means you treat every AI answer as a draft to test, ask what it might be getting wrong, and decide for yourself what to keep.

_items.title: Professional: responsible use at work
_items.body:
You bring AI into real work in a responsible, informed way. You decide when it fits a task and when it does not, direct it well, and stay in control of the quality and the final decisions.

At this level you can account for how you used it, keep within the rules of your field, and adapt as the tools change.
_items.advice: This means you can explain why you used AI, show that the judgement and the work were yours, and be trusted to use it well without being told how.

title: Worked example
instruction: Select the heading to open the worked example.

_items.title: Worked example
_items.body:
Consider two sport and exercise science students who each use a chatbot while writing a report.

Steffan types the question, reads the fluent answer, and pastes it into the report with a few words changed. It sounded expert, so Steffan submitted it as their own. But the brief never said AI was allowed, and the paragraph shows the tool's wording, not Steffan's understanding. Both the rule and the brief have been broken.

Mali checks the brief first to see whether AI is allowed and how. Mali then uses the tool only to get unstuck, rewrites the idea from their own understanding, and makes sure the finished work is theirs to explain and defend. The submitted work shows Mali's judgement, not the tool's.

Both students used the same chatbot. Only Mali kept the one rule: what you submit must be your own understanding, and the brief decides what is allowed.

title: Checking an AI answer
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These habits help you treat an AI answer as a prediction to check, not a fact to trust. Try them next time you use a chatbot.

_items.text: Have I checked my assignment brief to see whether AI is allowed here?

_items.feedback: Yes. That prediction is exactly what a generative AI tool does.

_items.text: It searches a fixed library and returns the stored, correct answer.
_items.feedback: A chatbot does not look up a stored answer; it predicts likely text.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the tool actually produces the words it gives you.

_items.text: Predicting the most likely wording for an answer, based on patterns in its training data.
_items.feedback: Yes. In sport as anywhere, the tool predicts likely text rather than retrieving a checked fact.

_items.text: Looking the idea up in sport textbooks and quoting the correct passage.
_items.feedback: It does not look up and quote a stored passage; it predicts wording.

_items.text: Checking its answer against the latest research in sport before replying.
_items.feedback: It does not verify its answer against current research before replying.

_items.text: Understanding sport the way your tutor does.
_items.feedback: It generates language without understanding your subject.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In sport, the tool predicts likely wording rather than looking the idea up or understanding it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The subject does not change what the tool is doing underneath.
_incorrect.final: Whatever the subject, the tool predicts likely wording from patterns. It does not look sport up, verify it, or understand it.

body: Generative AI produces fluent text by predicting likely patterns, not by understanding your topic or looking facts up, so it can be confidently wrong. This lesson is authored for the AI and Technology pathway and draws on the discussion of generative AI on page 184 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: When a brief allows AI, it does not allow it in one single way. Cardiff Met sets out three categories of AI use, and your assignment brief tells you which one applies to a given task. This lesson works through all three, so you can read a brief and know what is actually being asked of you.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You do not need to memorise policy wording. The aim is to recognise the three categories, tell what each one allows, and match a brief to the category it sets - because getting that right is what keeps your use of AI within the rules.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: name Cardiff Met's three categories of AI use and what each one allows
match an assignment brief to the category of AI use it sets
recognise that permission to use AI is never permission to submit AI's work as your own, in sport.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Cardiff Met describes three categories of AI use in assessment. Your assignment brief always tells you which one applies, so your first move is to read the brief.

Category 1 - No Use of Generative AI Expected. You produce the work from sources you have found and cited yourself. AI tools may be used only to check spelling, grammar and referencing.

Category 2 - AI Acknowledged. You may use AI to learn about your topic or to get initial guidance, such as a possible structure. Anything you take from it must be rewritten in your own words, integrated, referenced, and acknowledged in a short statement at the end.

Category 3 - AI Embedded. Using AI is an integral, expected part of the task. The brief sets out how to use it and how to acknowledge that use.

title: Concept: in practice
body: Whatever you are studying, the category is set by the brief, not by the subject. A brief in your field might set Category 1 and expect the work entirely in your own words, or Category 2 and let you take a structure from AI as long as you rewrite, reference and declare it. Reading the brief for its category is the habit that protects you. Permission to use AI, where it is given, is never permission to submit the tool's work as your own.

title: Explore the categories
displayTitle: The three categories of AI use
body: Cardiff Met sets three categories of AI use, and your assignment brief tells you which one applies. Open each level to see what it allows.
instruction: Open any level to read it. You can keep more than one open at once.

_items.title: Category 1: No AI expected
_items.body:
Your assignment should be produced using information sourced by you from your learning materials and academic sources, and cited appropriately.

AI tools for checking spelling, grammar and referencing may be used.
_items.advice: In practice: do your own reading and write in your own words. A spellchecker is fine. If you are unsure whether a tool counts as AI, ask your tutor before you use it.

_items.title: Category 2: AI acknowledged
_items.body:
You can use AI tools to learn about your topic, as part of your study, or in preparing initial guidance on assignments (for example a headline structure, or suggestions for topics to include).

Any materials you have sourced from AI should be rewritten or reconfigured, integrated into your own work, and referenced appropriately. Always confirm your findings with a relevant academic source.

Any support gained from AI should be acknowledged in a statement at the end of the assignment, making clear what the support was, and how you used it and developed it for your own work. Lesson 4 shows how to write that statement.
_items.advice: In practice: treat AI as a study partner, not a ghostwriter. Take its ideas, rewrite them yourself, check them against real sources, and add a short line saying what you used and how.

_items.title: Category 3: AI embedded
_items.body:
Use of AI is an integral and expected part of the assessment.

Because AI is explicitly included in the assessment, instructions on how you are expected to use it will be part of the assignment brief.

Your assignment brief will also describe how you should acknowledge the way you used AI tools.
_items.advice: In practice: the brief will spell out how to use AI and how to show your working. Follow it closely, and keep a record of your prompts and outputs as you go.

title: Worked example
instruction: Select the heading to open the worked example.

_items.title: Worked example
_items.body:
Consider two sport science students working to the same brief, writing a fitness-testing report, which sets Category 2: AI Acknowledged.

Nia skims the brief, sees that AI is allowed, and pastes a chatbot's draft into the work almost unchanged, with no acknowledgement. Category 2 asks for the ideas to be rewritten, referenced and declared, so Nia has gone beyond what the brief allows and is at risk of misconduct.

Trystan reads the brief properly, notes it is Category 2, and uses AI only to suggest a structure. Trystan then writes the work in their own words, references the sources, and adds a short statement of how AI was used. The same brief, done within its category.

Both were allowed to use AI. Only Trystan did what the category actually required.

title: Spotting an unreliable answer
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These checks help you judge when an AI answer can be trusted and when it cannot. Try them on your next answer.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I read the brief to see which of the three categories it sets?
If the brief says nothing about AI, have I treated it as Category 1 (none expected)?
For Category 2, have I rewritten anything from AI in my own words and referenced it?
For Category 2 or 3, have I written the acknowledgement the brief asks for?
Have I remembered that permission to use AI is not permission to submit its work as mine?

_items.text: Category 2: AI Acknowledged.
_items.feedback: Yes. Learn or get guidance from AI, then rewrite, reference and declare it.

_items.text: Category 1: No Use of Generative AI Expected.
_items.feedback: Category 1 allows AI only for spelling, grammar and referencing checks.

_items.text: Category 3: AI Embedded.
_items.feedback: Category 3 is where AI use is an integral, expected part of the task itself.

_items.text: None - any AI use here would be misconduct.
_items.feedback: The brief permits this use, so it is allowed when you rewrite, reference and declare it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Generative AI is strong at shaping and rewording language.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the task that is about wording, rather than about being right.
_incorrect.final: AI is strong at tasks about wording, such as rewording for clarity. It cannot guarantee facts, real references, or being up to date.

displayTitle: A brief in sport says nothing at all about AI. Which category should you assume, and what does it allow?

ariaQuestion: In the worked example, what did the second student do that kept them within the rules?

_items.text: Category 1: treat AI as not expected, and use it only to check spelling, grammar and referencing.
Category 3: AI is embedded, so use it freely across the task.
Category 2: use AI for anything, as long as you add a declaration.
Any category you like, because the brief did not rule AI out.

_feedback.correct: That's right. If the brief is silent, treat it as Category 1 and keep AI to spelling, grammar and referencing checks.

title: Formative check: why an answer can be wrong
displayTitle: You ask a chatbot a factual question about sport and it answers confidently. Why might that answer still be wrong?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why might a confident AI answer about your subject still be wrong?

_items.text: Because it predicts likely wording and can hallucinate facts, however confident it sounds.
_items.feedback: Yes. Confidence is no guarantee of accuracy in sport or anywhere.

_items.text: Because it always refuses to answer questions about sport.
_items.feedback: It does answer; the issue is that the answer may be false.

_items.text: Because confident answers from AI are always correct in sport.
_items.feedback: Confident answers are not always correct; that is the trap.

_items.text: Because it only works for essays, not for questions.
_items.feedback: It does answer questions; that is not why it can be wrong.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The tool predicts likely wording and can hallucinate, so a confident answer about sport can still be false.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the tool produces answers and why confidence is not proof.
_incorrect.final: A confident answer about sport can still be wrong because the tool predicts likely wording and can hallucinate facts.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

_items.title: This lesson is authored for the AI and Technology pathway and draws on the discussion of generative AI on page 184 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: Most students who get into trouble with AI did not set out to cheat. They drifted past a line they had not quite seen. This lesson shows you exactly where that line is, so you can stay the right side of it.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You do not need to learn the policy word for word. The aim is to recognise the behaviours Cardiff Met treats as academic misconduct, tell them apart from use a brief allows, and remember that the work you submit - and anything in it - is your responsibility.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise the AI-related behaviours Cardiff Met treats as academic misconduct
tell misconduct apart from use that an assignment brief allows
recognise that you are responsible for any AI error or bias you submit, in sport.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Academic integrity means being honest about what is your own work. Cardiff Met's rules name several AI-related behaviours as academic misconduct, whether or not you meant to break them:

Plagiarism - submitting AI-generated work or ideas as your own, without attribution.
Commissioning - using an AI tool to produce work you then submit as your own, even a free tool.
Fabrication - submitting invented material, such as fake references, made-up data or quotations the AI produced.
Collusion - several students using AI and handing in similar work, even unintentionally.
Substantial alteration - letting AI change your work well beyond a spelling or grammar check.
Prohibited sources - AI drawing on coursework-sharing sites without your knowledge, which can put you at risk.

The thread through all of them is simple: the work you submit must be your own, and you are responsible for anything in it, including any error or bias the tool introduced.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In your subject, the same line applies. You can learn from AI, and use it where a brief allows, but you cannot submit its work as your own or hand in material it invented. A fabricated reference or a confidently wrong claim becomes your responsibility the moment you include it. If several of you lean on the same tool and prompt, your work can end up looking alike, which can count as collusion even when no one intended it.

title: Spot the line
displayTitle: Misconduct, or allowed?
body: For each use of AI, predict whether it crosses the line. Turn the card to check.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over.

front.title: Pasting a chatbot's paragraph and submitting it as yours

back.title: Plagiarism
back.body: Submitting AI's words or ideas as your own, without attribution, is plagiarism. Write in your own words, and say where AI helped if your brief allows it.

front.title: Including a reference the AI gave you, without checking it exists

back.title: Fabrication
back.body: AI invents real-looking sources. Submitting one you have not verified is fabrication. Always find and read a source yourself before you cite it.

front.title: You and coursemates use the same prompt and hand in similar work

back.title: Collusion
back.body: Similar AI-produced work across students can count as collusion, even when unintended. Do your own thinking and write your own answer, even when you start from a shared idea.

front.title: Letting AI rewrite your whole draft, far beyond a grammar fix

back.title: Substantial alteration
back.body: Changes well beyond spelling and grammar mean the work is no longer your own. Keep AI to light checks unless your brief says you may use it for more.

front.title: Using AI to check spelling and grammar

back.title: Allowed
back.body: Category 1 permits AI for spelling, grammar and referencing checks. The thinking and the words stay yours.

front.title: Rewriting an AI idea in your own words, referencing and declaring it

back.title: Allowed
back.body: This is exactly what Category 2 asks for. You learn from AI, rewrite it yourself, and acknowledge the help.

title: Worked example
instruction: Select the heading to open the worked example.

_items.title: Worked example
_items.body:
Consider two sport science students using AI on the same report, where the brief sets Category 2.

Aled asks a chatbot to write a section, pastes it in with light edits, and keeps a journal reference the tool supplied. The reference turns out not to exist, and the writing is the tool's, not Aled's. That is plagiarism and fabrication, and Aled is responsible for both.

Seren uses the chatbot to suggest an angle, then writes the section in their own words, finds and checks real sources, and adds a short statement of how AI was used. Nothing is passed off, and nothing is invented.

Both used AI on a task that allowed it. Only Aled crossed the line into misconduct.

title: Using AI honestly
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These questions help you keep your use of AI within academic integrity. Run through them before you submit.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Is the thinking, and the final wording, still my own?
Have I avoided submitting AI-written text as if I wrote it?
Have I checked any AI reference or fact against a trusted source before using it?
If the brief allows AI, have I acknowledged it the way the brief requires?
Have I avoided shared or viral prompts that could make my work resemble others'?
Do I accept that I am responsible for any error or bias the tool introduced?

title: Formative check: what integrity asks
displayTitle: Which of these counts as academic misconduct?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these counts as academic misconduct?

_items.text: Submitting AI-written text as your own, without saying so.
_items.feedback: Yes. Passing off AI's work as your own is plagiarism.

_items.text: Using AI to check your spelling on a Category 1 task.
_items.feedback: That is allowed under Category 1.

_items.text: Rewriting an AI idea in your own words and referencing it on a Category 2 task.
_items.feedback: That is exactly what Category 2 permits.

_items.text: Asking AI to explain a concept so you understand it, then writing your own work.
_items.feedback: Learning from AI, then doing your own work, is fine.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic integrity asks you to be honest about what is your own and what the tool contributed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what integrity is really protecting.
_incorrect.final: Academic integrity asks you to be honest about your own work and the tool's part. It does not ban AI, reward secrecy, or allow the tool to do your reasoning.

title: Formative check: appropriate versus misconduct
displayTitle: On an assignment in sport, you paste an AI-written paragraph into your work and include a reference the AI gave you without checking it. Why is this misconduct?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: In the worked example, what made the first student's use misconduct while the second student's was not?

_items.text: You have submitted AI's work as your own and included an invented reference - plagiarism and fabrication.
It is not misconduct, because you edited a few words.
It is misconduct only if the reference happens to be wrong.
It is fine, as long as the tool you used was free.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Passing off AI's writing is plagiarism, and an unchecked invented reference is fabrication.

title: Formative check: acknowledging AI

_items.text: When your course asks you to, so it is clear what is yours and what the tool helped with.
_items.feedback: Yes. Acknowledging AI where your course asks keeps your use honest in sport.

_items.text: Never; using AI is something to keep to yourself.
_items.feedback: Keeping it secret is the opposite of academic integrity.

_items.text: Only if the final mark is low.
_items.feedback: Acknowledgement does not depend on your mark.

_items.text: Only if you used it to write the whole assignment.
_items.feedback: Acknowledgement is not limited to wholesale use.

_feedback.correct: That's right. You acknowledge AI use where your course asks, so it is clear what is yours and what the tool helped with.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what honesty requires, rather than what you could get away with.
_incorrect.final: You should acknowledge AI use when your course asks, so it is clear what is your own work and what the tool helped with.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Cardiff Met treats several AI-related behaviours as academic misconduct: plagiarism, commissioning, fabrication, collusion, substantial alteration, and using prohibited sources. The thread through all of them is that the work you submit must be your own, and you are responsible for anything in it, including any error or bias the tool introduced. Used within the category your brief sets, AI is fine; passing off its work, or handing in what it invented, is not. You can now recognise misconduct, tell it apart from allowed use, and see where your responsibility lies. The next lesson shows how to use AI honestly when a brief allows it, and how to declare it.

displayTitle: In plain terms, what does a generative AI tool do when you give it a prompt?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: In plain terms, what does a generative AI tool do with a prompt?

_items.text: It produces new text by predicting the most likely wording, piece by piece.
_items.feedback: Yes. It predicts likely wording rather than looking things up.

_items.text: It looks the answer up in a fixed, checked database.
_items.feedback: It does not retrieve a stored, checked answer.

_items.text: It understands the prompt the way a human expert would.
_items.feedback: It generates language without understanding.

_items.text: It copies a reply from a single trusted source.
_items.feedback: It predicts wording rather than copying one source.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A generative AI tool produces text by predicting the most likely wording.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the tool actually produces its words.

displayTitle: Which statement best describes how a chatbot produces its answer?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How does a chatbot produce its answer?

_items.text: By predicting likely patterns learned from large amounts of training data.
_items.feedback: Yes. Prediction from learned patterns is how it works.

_items.text: By searching the live internet and quoting the top result.
_items.feedback: It does not search and quote a live result.

_items.text: By reasoning from first principles like a scientist.
_items.feedback: It predicts wording rather than reasoning from principles.

_items.text: By retrieving a stored, pre-written answer for your question.
_items.feedback: The tool has no stored, pre-written answer to retrieve.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A chatbot predicts likely patterns from its training data.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Recall what the tool was trained to do.

displayTitle: A chatbot gives a confident, fluent answer that includes a made-up reference. What is this an example of?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A confident answer with a made-up reference is an example of what?

_items.text: A hallucination.
_items.feedback: Yes. A confident, false statement from AI is a hallucination.

_items.text: A search result.
_items.feedback: The tool did not search; it invented the reference.

_items.text: A citation.
_items.feedback: A real citation points to a source that exists.

_items.text: A summary.
_items.feedback: This is an invented fact, not a summary.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A confident, false statement like an invented reference is a hallucination.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What do we call it when AI states something false with confidence?

displayTitle: Which task is generative AI least reliable at on its own?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which task is generative AI least reliable at on its own?

_items.text: Giving accurate facts and real references.
_items.feedback: Yes. Facts and references are where it is least reliable.

_items.text: Rewording a sentence to make it clearer.
_items.feedback: Rewording is a strength, not a weakness.

_items.text: Suggesting an outline for an essay.
_items.feedback: Suggesting structure is something it does well.

_items.text: Explaining an idea in simpler words.
_items.feedback: Explaining in simpler words is a strength.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Generative AI is least reliable at accurate facts and real references.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the task where being right matters most.

displayTitle: Which use of an AI tool is most likely to count as academic misconduct?

ariaQuestion: Which use of AI is most likely to count as misconduct?

_items.text: Submitting AI-written reasoning as if it were your own work.
_items.feedback: Yes. Passing off the tool's reasoning as your own is misconduct.

_items.text: Asking it to explain a difficult idea you then write up yourself.
_items.feedback: That is an acceptable study-aid use.

_items.text: Using it to check your grammar.
_items.feedback: Checking grammar is generally acceptable.

_items.text: Asking it to suggest a structure you then fill in yourself.
_items.feedback: Suggesting a structure you fill in is acceptable.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Submitting AI-written reasoning as your own is academic misconduct.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option passes off the tool's work as the student's own?

displayTitle: You used an AI tool to help plan an essay. What does academic integrity ask you to do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: After using AI to help plan an essay, what does integrity ask?

_items.text: Keep the thinking and words your own, and acknowledge the tool where your course asks.
_items.feedback: Yes. Keep the work yours and be open about the tool.

_items.text: Hide that you used it so no one can object.
_items.feedback: Hiding use is the opposite of integrity.

_items.text: Let the tool write the essay since you planned it together.
_items.feedback: The writing and reasoning should stay your own.

_items.text: Nothing; AI use never needs acknowledging.
_items.feedback: Many courses do ask you to acknowledge AI use.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Keep the thinking and words your own, and acknowledge the tool where your course asks.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about honesty and whose work the essay should be.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Generative AI is no longer a mystery box: it is a tool you can describe and use with care. You can explain what it is, something that produces likely patterns from data rather than a mind or a search engine. You can describe what it does well and where it fails, and why a confident answer can still be wrong. And you can recognise how to use it honestly, acknowledging it where you should. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, these tools are something you use with judgement in every part of your sport studies. Each time you ask an AI for help, check its answer against the evidence rather than trust it, and declare its use where your course requires, you are putting this course to work. It matters beyond your degree too: using AI honestly and knowing its limits is fast becoming an everyday skill in sport research, coaching and professional practice.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced AI and Technology courses take you into using AI on real study tasks, and then into evaluating tools, creating with them and reasoning about the wider ethics. Going wider: the same judgement underpins Criticality, Academic Writing and Referencing, where you weigh sources, write in your own voice and acknowledge your sources properly.

title: Orientation
body: You now know what AI is, the one rule, the three categories, and where misconduct begins. This final lesson brings it together: when a brief allows AI, how do you actually use it honestly - and prove that you did?

title: Orientation: at this level
body: The aim here is practical. Follow a clear six-step process for using AI on work that allows it, write a declaration that stands up, and keep an evidence trail - so your use is honest and you can show it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: follow Cardiff Met's six-step process for using AI honestly on work that allows it
write an AI declaration that acknowledges, describes and evidences your use
assemble an evidence trail that shows the work is your own, in sport.

title: Concept: definition
body:
When your assignment brief allows AI, there is an honest way to use it that keeps the work yours. Cardiff Met sets out a six-step process: think first, design your prompt, develop the dialogue, critically evaluate the output, log your use, and check for red flags before you submit.

Two habits sit alongside the process. You declare your AI use, and you keep an evidence trail. A good declaration has three parts - Acknowledge the tool and its publisher, Describe how you used it, and Evidence the interaction with your prompts and the outputs. An evidence trail is the dated drafts, research notes and saved AI chats that show the work developed as your own.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In your subject, the honest process is the same. You start from your own view of the task, use AI within the category your brief sets, and treat everything it gives you as a draft to check, not an answer to submit. You log what you did as you go, so the declaration almost writes itself. The evidence trail - your dated drafts, notes and saved chats - is what shows, if anyone asks, that the work and the thinking are yours.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the next assignment where you might use AI. Which of the six steps would you be most tempted to skip, and what would you write in your declaration?

title: The six steps as one process
displayTitle: The six steps as one process
body: When a brief allows AI, this is the honest way to use it. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Think first
_items.body: Note your own position on the task before you open any AI tool, so your thinking leads.

_items.title: Design the prompt
_items.body: Build a prompt that gives the tool a role, a clear task, and the context it needs.

_items.title: Develop it
_items.body: Treat the first answer as a draft. Ask for alternatives, examples and challenges; prompting is iterative.

_items.title: Evaluate
_items.body: Fact-check claims, verify sources, watch for bias, and compare against your own reading.

_items.title: Log your use
_items.body: Record what you used AI for, how, and the outputs, ready for your declaration.

_items.title: Red-flag check
_items.body: Before submitting, check nothing crosses the line, such as unacknowledged AI text or changed meaning.

title: Worked example
instruction: Select the heading to open the worked example.

_items.title: Worked example
_items.body:
Consider two sport science students, writing a report whose brief allows AI as Category 2.

Teleri skips the planning, asks a chatbot to write a section, and pastes it in with light edits. Teleri keeps a reference the tool supplied without checking it, writes no record of the use, and adds no declaration. The work is the tool’s, a source may be invented, and nothing shows Teleri’s own understanding.

Cai thinks first and notes a line of argument, then uses the tool to suggest an angle, not a finished answer. Cai fact-checks every claim against real sources, keeps the chat and the drafts, and writes a short declaration naming the tool, how it was used, and the prompts and outputs.

Both had the same permission. Only Cai used AI honestly and could show the work was their own.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to use AI with your eyes open
body: Run through these each time you use an AI tool, so the three ideas stay joined up.

_items.text: Have I declared my AI use, naming the tool and its publisher with a URL?
Does my declaration describe how I used the tool and why?
Have I kept evidence of the interaction - the prompts I used and the outputs?
Have I saved dated drafts that show how the work developed?
Did I screenshot or export any AI chats at the time I used them?
Could I show that the thinking and the words are my own?

displayTitle: In Cardiff Met's six-step process, what should you do before you open an AI tool?
body: Why is it better to treat these three ideas as one practice rather than three separate facts to recall?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: In Cardiff Met's six-step process, what should you do before you open an AI tool?

_items.text: Think first: note your own position on the task, so your thinking leads.
_items.feedback: Yes. Step one is your own thinking, before any tool.

_items.text: Paste the assignment title in and accept the first answer.
_items.feedback: That hands your thinking to the tool; step one is to form your own view.

_items.text: Ask the tool to write the whole piece, then edit it.
_items.feedback: That is not the honest process, and likely crosses into misconduct.

_items.text: Decide which reference you will fabricate.
_items.feedback: Fabrication is misconduct; the process keeps the work honest.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three ideas only protect your learning when you use them together, each time you reach for a tool.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you gain by applying all three ideas at the same time.

displayTitle: You have used AI within the category your brief allows on an assignment in sport. What is the best way to be ready if anyone questions the work?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A good AI declaration always does three things. Which option names them?

_items.text: Keep an evidence trail - dated drafts, notes, and AI chats saved at the time - and declare your use.
Delete the AI chats so there is nothing to find.
Say nothing about AI and hope it is not noticed.
Rewrite everything at the last minute to look different.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An evidence trail plus a clear declaration is your strongest protection.

displayTitle: You want to use AI well while studying sport this term. Which plan best brings the three ideas together?
body: You want to use AI well while studying sport this term. Which plan best brings the three ideas together?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use AI well while studying your subject this term. Which plan best brings the three ideas together?

_items.text: Each time you use a tool, remember what it is, check anything that must be right, and keep your work honest.
_items.feedback: Yes. That applies all three ideas together, every time.

_items.text: Use AI for everything and trust it, since it sounds confident and saves time.
_items.feedback: A confident tone is no guarantee of accuracy. This skips checking and honesty.

_items.text: Only worry about using AI honestly, and skip understanding or checking it.
_items.feedback: Honesty alone will not catch a hallucinated fact. All three ideas are needed.

_items.text: Avoid AI completely so you never have to think about any of this.
_items.feedback: Avoiding it is one choice, but the practice is about using AI well when you do.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Using AI well means applying all three ideas together, each time you pick up a tool.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan uses understanding, checking and honesty all together.

displayTitle: What does it mean to use generative AI with your eyes open?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to use generative AI with your eyes open?

_items.text: To bring together understanding the tool, checking what it says, and using it honestly, each time you use it.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three ideas, applied together.

_items.text: To use it as much as possible, since it is faster than doing the work yourself.
_items.feedback: Speed is not the point, and this skips checking and honesty.

_items.text: To trust its answers fully, because it writes in a confident, expert style.
_items.feedback: A confident style is no guarantee that an answer is right.

_items.text: To avoid it entirely until someone teaches you every rule.
_items.feedback: The practice is about using AI well, not avoiding it.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

_items.text: Only the speed; the essay simply took too long to finish.
_items.feedback: Speed is not the issue. Checking and honesty are what went missing.

_items.text: Nothing important, as long as the final essay reads well.

title: Decide what is allowed
displayTitle: Decide what is allowed
body: Your brief sets the category. Read the situation and choose what to do.
instruction: Choose a response to see what happens, then follow where it leads. Each choice has consequences.

n1.body: Your essay brief says "Category 2 - AI Acknowledged". You are stuck on how to structure your argument. What do you do?

_choices.text: Ask AI for a possible structure, then write the essay yourself.
_choices.consequence: A sound start. The argument stays yours - but under Category 2 the job is not finished once the essay is written.

_choices.text: Ask AI to write the essay, then change a few words and submit it.
_choices.consequence: That is commissioning: the argument is the tool's, not yours. You still have time before the deadline, though.

_choices.text: Avoid AI altogether, because you are unsure.
_choices.consequence: Safe, but your brief actually permits AI guidance. It is worth re-reading what it allows.

n2.body: You have written the essay in your own words, using the AI's outline only as a starting point. Before you submit, what do you do about the AI's help?

_choices.text: Add an acknowledgement of what the AI did and how you used it, and check its suggestions against a reliable source.
_choices.consequence: Exactly right: honest use, acknowledged and confirmed.

_choices.text: Say nothing, because the final writing is all mine now.
_choices.consequence: The writing is yours, but Category 2 asks you to acknowledge the help. Leaving it out is still a breach.

_choices.text: Acknowledge the help, but do not bother checking what the AI suggested.
_choices.consequence: Better, but AI can be fluent and wrong. An unchecked claim can cost you marks or accuracy.

nRecover.body: The essay is really the tool's work, not yours. What now?

_choices.text: Submit it anyway, since it is done.
_choices.consequence: You decide to hand in the tool's work as your own.

_choices.text: Start again and build the argument yourself, using AI only for guidance.
_choices.consequence: A good recovery. That is what Category 2 asks of you.

nReread.body: You re-read the brief. It clearly allows AI guidance as long as you acknowledge it. What do you do?

_choices.text: Use AI for a structure, then write the essay yourself and acknowledge it.
_choices.consequence: Now you are taking the help the brief allows.

_choices.text: Still avoid AI, just to be safe.
_choices.consequence: No breach - but you have turned down help you are allowed to use.

nGood.body: Category 2 done well: you learned from AI, kept the argument yours, acknowledged and referenced the help, and confirmed it against a reliable source.

nPoorAck.body: Using AI help without acknowledging it is misconduct under Category 2, even when the final words are yours. Add the acknowledgement before you submit.

nNeutralAck.body: You acknowledged the help, which is right. Next time, check the AI's suggestions against a reliable source too: fluent does not mean correct.

nPoor.body: Submitting AI-written work as your own is misconduct, whatever the category. The argument has to be yours.

nNeutral.body: Reading the brief closely shows what you may do. Staying over-cautious means passing up help you are allowed to use.

title: Six ways AI use becomes misconduct
displayTitle: Six named behaviours
body: Cardiff Met's rules name these AI-related behaviours as academic misconduct, whether or not you meant to break them.

_items.title: Plagiarism
_items.text: Submitting AI-generated work or ideas as your own, without attribution.

_items.title: Commissioning
_items.text: Using an AI tool to produce work you then submit as your own, even a free tool.

_items.title: Fabrication
_items.text: Submitting invented material, such as fake references, made-up data or quotations the AI produced.

_items.title: Collusion
_items.text: Several students using AI and handing in similar work, even unintentionally.

_items.title: Substantial alteration
_items.text: Letting AI change your work well beyond a spelling or grammar check.

_items.title: Prohibited sources
_items.text: AI drawing on coursework-sharing sites without your knowledge, which can put you at risk.

title: Put honest AI use in order
displayTitle: Put honest AI use in order
body: These are the steps of using AI honestly and showing it. Put them in the order you would follow them.
instruction: Drag the steps into the right order, then select Submit.

_items.text: Read the brief to find which AI category applies.
Use AI only in the way that category allows.
Rewrite anything you take from AI in your own words.
Check every fact and reference the AI gave you.
Add a short acknowledgement of how you used AI.

_feedback.title: The honest-use sequence
_feedback.correct: That is the order. Read the brief first, stay within the category, rewrite, check, then acknowledge.

_incorrect.final: Not quite. The brief comes first, then careful use, then rewriting, checking and acknowledging.
_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what has to happen before you can write anything down, and try again.
